title: Gujarat Lung Cancer Cases Surge as State's Tobacco Acreage Keeps Expanding
excerpt: GCRI treated 55% more lung cancer patients in 2024 than in 2020, while Gujarat's tobacco cultivation area grew 20% to over 200,000 hectares despite the Centre's crop diversification push.
body:
• Gujarat Cancer and Research Institute treated 1,086 lung cancer patients in 2024, up 55% from 700 in 2020, with 4,397 total cases over five years
  • Gujarat's tobacco cultivation area expanded 20% from 170,000 to 205,000 hectares between 2020 and 2025, despite a central government diversification programme running since 2015
  • Over 40% of lung cancer cases in India are diagnosed at advanced stages, and tobacco remains the leading risk factor, according to GCRI officials

Lung cancer cases at Gujarat's premier oncology centre have climbed sharply over five years, even as the state's tobacco farming footprint expanded to its largest in at least a decade — a dual trend that undercuts New Delhi's efforts to wean farmers off the crop and reduce tobacco-related disease.

The Gujarat Cancer and Research Institute in Ahmedabad treated 1,086 lung cancer patients in 2024, up from 700 in 2020 — a 55% increase, according to data released on World Lung Cancer Day on August 1. The institute handled 4,397 lung cancer cases between 2020 and 2024, with men accounting for 3,597 of those patients and women for 799.

"Awareness is our greatest defence. Early detection, quitting tobacco, and timely care can save lives."

— Dr Shashank Pandya, Director, Gujarat Cancer and Research Institute

Tobacco Cultivation Defies Diversification Push

Parliamentary data tabled in the Lok Sabha in February 2026 reveals that Gujarat's tobacco acreage rose from 170,450 hectares in 2020-21 to 204,790 hectares in 2024-25 — a 20% expansion. Production followed a similar trajectory, climbing from 396,190 tonnes to 468,970 tonnes over the same period.

Gujarat now accounts for roughly 45% of India's total tobacco output, anchored in the Charotar belt around Kheda and Anand districts. The state's dominance has grown even as the Centre's Crop Diversification Programme, implemented under PM-RKVY across 10 tobacco-growing states since 2015-16, allocated approximately ₹3 crore annually to Gujarat to encourage farmers to shift to alternative crops. Only 13,858 hectares in Gujarat have transitioned away from tobacco under the programme — less than 7% of the state's current tobacco area.

A Health Crisis Compounding

The rising caseload at GCRI reflects a broader pattern. In Gujarat, approximately 98 men and 78 women per lakh population are diagnosed with lung cancer, and the disease accounts for 15% of all cancer cases in the state, according to data cited by Apollo Hospitals Ahmedabad.

GCRI officials stressed that over 40% of lung cancer cases nationally are caught at advanced stages, when treatment options narrow and survival rates drop. The institute urged high-risk individuals — long-term smokers and those exposed to environmental pollutants — to undergo low-dose CT scans for early screening.

Of the 4,397 patients GCRI treated over five years, 3,256 received care under the PMJAY-MA Ayushman Bharat health insurance scheme. Another 1,426 patients travelled from other Indian states, a figure GCRI cites as evidence of Gujarat's growing role as a national cancer care hub. The institute deploys technologies including CyberKnife, robotic surgery, and PET-CT scanning.

Meanwhile, a separate AIIMS study noted that nearly 40% of India's estimated 100,000 annual lung cancer cases now occur in non-smokers, driven by air pollution and PM 2.5 exposure — adding another dimension to the challenge beyond tobacco control.

The Diaspora Connection

Gujarat's infrastructure has also attracted Non-Resident Gujaratis seeking affordable, high-quality cancer treatment. The state's medical tourism sector has grown at 33% annually, outpacing the national average of 20%, with Ahmedabad, Vadodara, and Surat emerging as key destinations. Affordable procedures, streamlined medical visa support, and cashless facilities make Gujarat increasingly accessible for overseas patients from the diaspora, Africa, SAARC nations, and the Middle East.

What's Next

The divergence between rising tobacco cultivation and climbing cancer cases poses a policy dilemma for both the Centre and the Gujarat state government. Tobacco farmers in the Charotar region have pushed back against recent tax increases — the Centre raised GST on tobacco products to 40% from 28% and imposed an additional excise duty — warning that the combined burden could drive small growers out of business. Yet the public health data suggests the economic calculus of tobacco farming carries costs that extend well beyond the farm gate.

GCRI's World Lung Cancer Day appeal for early screening and tobacco cessation lands at a moment when India's tobacco sector and its health consequences are expanding in parallel — a gap that neither crop diversification funding nor awareness campaigns have yet managed to close.
